Crimes Oubliés raconte des affaires crim: Crimes Oubliés ("Forgotten Crimes") tells old criminal cases, from before DNA, CCTV and modern forensics. Each case is handled like an investigation and placed back in its historical, economic and social context: the crime is the way in, the real subject is the era. Behind the mic, Camille Debreuille writes, narrates and produces alone, since September 2023. By day, she runs Agence Spotted, which makes podcasts for brands. By night, she tells murder stories.
Plus de 200 épisodes et 39 saisons plus: More than 200 episodes and 39 seasons later, the show claims over a million listens and holds 4.7 out of 5 on Apple Podcasts. It places itself in the lineage of Hondelatte raconte, Affaires sensibles and Pierre Bellemare's stories. Same library, different shelf. In spring 2026 her book came out, Crimes oubliés : cinq affaires criminelles, cinq familles anéanties (L'Oiseau Noir, 288 pages), which opens with the Lizzie Borden case.
Pas de téléphone, pas de caméra, pas de: No phone, no camera, no lab finding a hair at the end: witnesses, rumours, confessions, and investigators making do with what they have. To understand a crime from 1900, you have to understand poverty, family, the village, what a woman or a worker risked.
Une bande-annonce, puis trois épisodes d: A trailer, then three episodes of about eighteen minutes, and often a full-length bonus. The length of a metro ride: you get on at the start of the case and get off with a suspect.
Une seule personne à l'écriture, au réci: One person writing, narrating and producing, every week for more than two years, with very professional production. In October 2026, the show moved from Ausha to Acast, which lives off advertising.
Lolo, auditeur assidu qui avait proposé: Lolo, a loyal listener who had pitched the show eleven times, PowerPoint in hand, argued the case in the absence of Steph, our true crime specialist. Verdict: it's serious, precise, well researched, well told, and it turns a crime story into a history lesson. Over a million listens without a big label behind it is quite a feat, even if it doesn't pay much. Where to start: a three-part case, from the beginning, over three commutes. The Weidmann case if you want something famous, otherwise one you've never heard of, like Joseph Vacher's: that's where the name really makes sense.
Deux réserves et demie, pourtant. Le nom: Two and a half reservations, though. The name, first: Mary Bell, Ruth Ellis (the last woman hanged in the UK, posthumously pardoned in July 2026), Weidmann or Lizzie Borden are only forgotten by some listeners, not by History. The titles, next: the storytelling keeps its "no voyeurism" promise, the shop window goes for the hook, and an exclamation mark in a case with people dead grates. Behind these cases there are real victims, and the show respects them in the storytelling, a little less in some titles. And the half: splitting stories in three builds loyalty, but at the release pace it takes three weeks to learn the ending. And the music is sometimes a bit too present.
